title: How Money Is Earned
concept: People usually earn money by doing work, selling useful products, or providing services that create value for others.
learningObjective: Understand the different ways people can earn money by creating value for someone else.
primaryMisconception: Money only comes from salaries or parents.
secondaryMisconceptions: A person must have a formal job to earn money.
Waiting for someone to give you money is the same as earning it.
keyTakeaway: Money is usually earned by creating value for someone.

screens.title: An Empty Saving Jar
screens.content: You want a £12 sketchbook, but your saving jar is empty. Which choice would help you earn the money?
screens.illustration: A student looks at a £12 sketchbook beside an empty saving jar. Four mystery-path icons appear behind them.

screens.title: Four Possible Paths
screens.content: Ayaan could help at his family’s shop, sell his drawings, tutor another student, or wait for his next pocket-money day.
screens.illustration: Four path cards show a shop shelf, a drawing, two students studying, and a calendar beside a pocket-money jar.

screens.title: Money Arrives Differently
screens.content: Some choices require effort, skills, or something useful to offer. One choice only requires waiting. Will every path count as earning?
screens.illustration: Three paths show an exchange symbol between Ayaan and another person. The waiting path shows only a clock.

screens.title: What Makes It Earning?
screens.question: Which clue best shows that money was earned?

options.text: Someone received useful value in return
options.response: Good thinking. Earning usually involves providing work, a product, or a service that someone values.

options.text: The money came from an adult
options.response: Adults can pay for work, but they can also give gifts or pocket money.

options.text: The money was given as coins
options.response: The form of the money does not show whether it was earned.
Waiting may lead to receiving money, but it does not automatically mean the money was earned.

screens.title: Choose Ayaan’s Money Path
screens.instruction: Explore all four choices. Follow each path and decide whether Ayaan earns money or simply receives it.

startingNode.content: Ayaan wants to collect £12 for a sketchbook. An adult has approved three safe, age-appropriate ways he could try to earn part of the money.

choices.label: Help at the family shop
choices.description: Help organise greeting cards at the family shop.
choices.consequence: Ayaan spends one hour sorting the cards. The organised display saves the shopkeeper time. The family agrees to pay him £4.

choices.label: Sell drawings
choices.description: Offer two original drawings for sale with an adult’s permission.
choices.consequence: Two people enjoy the drawings and agree to buy them for £3 each. Ayaan receives £6.

choices.label: Tutor another student
choices.description: Help a younger student practise multiplication with both families’ permission.
choices.consequence: Ayaan explains the questions clearly for 30 minutes. The other student improves, and the family pays Ayaan £5.

choices.label: Wait for pocket money
choices.description: Wait until his family’s next pocket-money day.
choices.consequence: Ayaan receives £3 from his family. In this path, he did not complete an agreed task, sell a product, or provide a service.

options.text: No, it was received rather than directly earned

terminalOutcomes.title: Earned through work
terminalOutcomes.content: Ayaan created value by completing a useful task and earned £4.

terminalOutcomes.title: Earned by selling a product
terminalOutcomes.content: Ayaan created something people valued and earned £6.

terminalOutcomes.title: Earned by providing a service
terminalOutcomes.content: Ayaan used his time and skill to help someone and earned £5.

terminalOutcomes.title: Money received
terminalOutcomes.content: The £3 still helps Ayaan, but this particular payment was given rather than directly earned.

config.validationMethod: Check each branch after its follow-up choice. Complete the interaction when all four paths have been explored and correctly identified.
config.retryBehavior: Keep completed branches marked. Return the learner to the current follow-up node, provide one short hint, and allow unlimited retries.

accessibilityAlternative.method: Present the tree as a numbered list of four choices. Each branch opens as a linear text sequence with selectable buttons.
accessibilityAlternative.screenReaderInstruction: Choose a path, listen to its consequence, identify how the money arrived, and return to explore the remaining paths.

tradeOffSummary: Work requires time and effort, and the task must be safe and useful.
A product requires something another person wants and may require materials.
A service requires time, skill, and someone who needs the help.
Pocket money depends on the giver and may be received without creating value in return.
There is no single best earning path. Available choices depend on skills, permission, safety, time, and what other people value.

feedback.success: Great exploring. Ayaan can earn money through work, products, or services. Pocket money can be useful, but receiving it is not always the same as earning it.
feedback.incorrect: Look for the exchange. Did Ayaan provide useful work, a product, or a service in return for the money?
feedback.incomplete: Explore every path before finishing the decision tree.

screens.title: Creating Value Can Earn Money
screens.content: You explored four paths. Shop work created value through a useful task. Drawings created value as products. Tutoring created value as a service. These are ways of earning money: receiving payment because someone values what you did or provided. Waiting for pocket money may still bring money, but it is received rather than directly earned. A salary is one way to earn, not the only way. Children’s activities should always be safe and approved by an adult.
screens.simpleSummary: You earn by offering work, products, or services people value.
screens.illustration: Three arrows labelled Work, Product, and Service lead toward an earning jar. A separate Money Received arrow leads from a gift box.

screens.title: The Plant-Watering Helper
screens.content: With a parent’s permission, Lily waters a neighbour’s plants while the neighbour is away. The neighbour agrees to pay her £5. Lily does not have a formal job or salary, but she earns money by providing a useful service.
screens.illustration: Lily waters several plants while a parent watches nearby. A neighbour thanks her and places £5 in her saving jar.

questions.text: Theo helps organise books for a school fair and receives an agreed payment of £4. How did he earn it?

options.feedback: Correct. Theo completed a useful task in return for the agreed payment.
Theo did more than wait. He completed a useful task in return for the payment.
The £4 was connected to the work he completed, so it was not a birthday gift.
Borrowed money must usually be returned. Theo received payment for his work.

questions.correctExplanation: Theo completed a useful task that helped prepare the school fair. The agreed payment was earned through work.
questions.misconceptionTested: Waiting for someone to give you money is the same as earning it.

questions.text: Which statement about earning money is correct?

options.text: People can earn through work, products, or services
options.feedback: Correct. Salaries are only one of several ways people can earn money.

options.text: Only people with salaries can earn money
options.feedback: A formal salary is not required. A person may earn from a useful task, product, or service.
Parents may give money, but people can also earn it by creating value for others.
A gift can be received without work, a product, or a service being provided in return.

questions.correctExplanation: A salary is one form of earning, but people can also earn by completing useful work, selling products, or providing services.
questions.misconceptionTested: Money only comes from salaries or parents.

questions.text: Amelia wants to earn £8. Which choice directly creates value for someone else?

options.text: Offer to organise craft supplies for an agreed payment
options.feedback: Correct. Organising the supplies is useful work that creates value.
Birthday money may be received, but waiting for it is not directly earning it.
Receiving money after asking is different from earning it through work, a product, or a service.

options.text: Look at the saving jar each day
options.feedback: Watching the jar does not create value or increase the money inside it.

questions.correctExplanation: Organising the supplies is useful work. If an adult agrees to pay for the task, Amelia earns money by creating value.
questions.misconceptionTested: A person must have a formal job to earn money.

screens.headline: Value Creator!
screens.message: You discovered that money can be earned through useful work, products, and services—not only salaries.
screens.progressMessage: Mission 3 complete in Become Money Smart.
screens.nextMissionTeaser: Next, explore what happens when money is spent, saved, or shared.
screens.animation: Work, drawing, and tutoring icons drop coins into a saving jar. The jar fills to £12 and gives a gentle sparkle.

screens.title: Find the Value
screens.instruction: Think of three people you know. Identify one useful task, product, or service each person provides. No selling or payment is required.

reviewChecklist.notes: The mission focuses on how money is earned by creating value through work, products, or services.
The mission distinguishes earned money from gifts or pocket money received without an agreed exchange.
The examples use drawings, tutoring, pocket money, school fairs, saving jars, and safe family situations.
The mission does not discuss investing.
The mission does not discuss financial returns.
The mission does not discuss stocks or market prices.
Receiving pocket money is not described as wrong or less valuable. It is simply distinguished from directly earning money.
The mission explains that payment depends on agreement, usefulness, safety, permission, and what another person values.
The mission uses pounds, pocket money, a family shop, drawings, tutoring, and school-related activities familiar to UK learners.
The learner explores work, product, service, and received-money paths and identifies how money arrives in each case.
The questions address salaries, parents, formal jobs, gifts, waiting, and value creation.

reviewChecklist.item: Mission can be completed in under five minutes
reviewChecklist.notes: The mission uses two short story screens, four concise decision branches, and three quiz questions.

reviewChecklist.item: Language matches the target reading level
reviewChecklist.notes: The language is concrete, encouraging, and suitable for children aged 8–12.
